The best thing about being an immigrant in the U.S. is that it opens the doors to Latin America

Kiran Desai, the acclaimed Indian-born author living in the United States, found inspiration for her ambitious latest novel along Mexico's Pacific coast. The 54-year-old writer, who became the youngest Booker Prize winner two decades ago, has spent extended periods in various Mexican regions with her mother, also a novelist. In the beach town of La Manzanilla, Jalisco, Desai discovered a powerful metaphor: loneliness is as capricious and changeable as water itself. Her nearly 700-page novel, "The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny," explores love on the surface but delves deeper into the complexities of our globalized world, where migration, culture, and colonialism can be both blessing and curse. Desai sees profound connections between Mexico and India that go far beyond superficial similarities like spicy food. Both countries contain living ancient civilizations where multiple time periods seem to exist simultaneously, she observes. Both grapple with colonial legacies that persist today, operating not just from outside forces but within their own societies across class lines. The interview also reveals Desai's nuanced relationship with literary labels. While she counts Juan Rulfo and Gabriel García Márquez among her influences, she critiques how "magical realism" has been applied almost exclusively to writers from poorer countries, never to European or American authors exploring similar themes. This story offers a thoughtful glimpse into how artists find unexpected resonances across cultures and how physical places can unlock creative understanding about universal human experiences like solitude and belonging.

First responders awarded decades after Australia's worst rail crash

Nearly fifty years after Australia's worst rail disaster, the first responders who worked tirelessly to save lives are finally receiving formal recognition. On January 18, 1977, a passenger train derailed in Granville, Sydney, its carriages crushed beneath a collapsed bridge. What began as a suspected hoax call became a catastrophic scene: 85 people killed, including two unborn babies, and more than 200 injured. Ambulance officer Barry Gobbe and police officer Gary Raymond were among the first to arrive, confronting the surreal horror of passengers frozen mid-commute, cards and magazines still in hand. The rescue effort stretched until evening, with Raymond at one point crawling through the wreckage to reach trapped passengers. When ordered to evacuate due to collapse fears, he left a small pen torch with survivor Debbie Woodgate—a gesture that later guided him back to her through the darkness. That connection endured; Raymond and Woodgate remain friends nearly five decades later. The disaster prompted sweeping reforms in emergency response protocols, including color-coded helmets to identify personnel, and advanced medical understanding of crush syndrome, a then-obscure condition affecting seven survivors. This story matters not only as a tribute to courage under unimaginable pressure, but as a reminder of how tragedy can catalyze lasting change. The 2026 Australian Bravery Decorations honor Gobbe, Raymond, and the late Superintendent Richard Lamb, who rushed to the scene on his day off. Yet the recipients insist the recognition belongs to all who helped that day—the thousands of emergency workers, volunteers, and tradespeople who turned a nightmare into a moment of collective human resilience.

Environmental crimes don’t stop at borders. Neither can the reporting

Environmental crimes like illegal gold mining and wildlife trafficking don't respect borders, and neither should the journalism that exposes them. That's the philosophy driving Daniela Quintero, investigations editor at Mongabay Latam, who is pioneering cross-border collaborations to document the complex networks behind nature crimes across Latin America. Quintero's approach blends traditional field reporting with modern investigative tools—satellite imagery, environmental databases, legal documents, and scientific literature. A recent investigation she coordinated tracked how illegal Amazonian gold was being laundered through Venezuela after Brazil tightened trade controls, a story that required journalists in three countries working in concert. Beyond her editing work, Quintero coordinates Mongabay's Nature Crimes Fellowship, training senior journalists from Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru to develop investigative skills focused on environmental reporting in the Amazon and Pacific regions. The Colombian journalist and sociologist came to Mongabay in early 2025 after years covering environmental issues at El Espectador, one of Colombia's oldest newspapers. This profile, captured during an interview in Colombia's Guainía department ahead of a Mongabay conference, offers a window into what investigative environmental journalism looks like in practice. Quintero's work reminds us that understanding today's environmental challenges requires following the threads across borders, combining boots-on-the-ground reporting with data analysis, and building networks of journalists who can see the whole picture. It's a quiet but essential evolution in how we document and ultimately address crimes against nature.

Scientists use satellites to track whale strandings in remote places from space

In 2015, 337 sei whales washed ashore along Chile's remote Patagonian coast in what became the largest recorded mass baleen whale mortality event. The most striking detail? Nobody discovered the stranding for two months. This tragedy became a turning point for marine science, demonstrating both the vastness of our ocean blindspots and the potential of satellite technology to help fill them. Scientists now use very high-resolution orbital imagery to monitor whale strandings in the world's most inaccessible places, transforming what were once unidentifiable dark blobs in early 2000s satellite photos into detailed images that reveal species, decomposition stages, and even individual scars. Penny Clarke and her colleagues at the British Antarctic Survey have been at the forefront of this effort since 2019, part of a growing global network using digital eyes in the sky to track cetaceans. The technology allows researchers to distinguish flippers and flukes, estimate whale size, and differentiate calves from adults. With whale strandings rising significantly in some regions over the past two decades, this capability has become invaluable for understanding mortality patterns, sea surface temperatures, and ocean currents in remote areas. Scientists emphasize that satellites complement rather than replace traditional fieldwork, as cloud cover, wind, and satellite availability can limit data quality. This story offers a quiet reminder of how technology can extend our care across distances we cannot physically reach. The long-term goal is to develop automated detection systems that spot strandings quickly enough to intervene and identify causes, turning orbital observation into an early-warning system for ocean health and the creatures that depend on it.

Federal Prosecutors Request Immediate Creation of Committee to Manage Upper Paraguay Basin

Brazil's Federal Public Prosecutor's Office has filed an urgent lawsuit demanding the immediate creation of a management committee for the Upper Paraguay River Basin, the waterway that feeds the Pantanal, the world's largest tropical wetland. The legal action targets federal and state governments, arguing that the absence of this coordinating body has left one of South America's most important ecosystems vulnerable to fragmented decision-making and unchecked industrial development. At the heart of the case is concern over major infrastructure projects, including the Paraguay-Paraná Waterway—a series of dredging operations, port terminals, and channel deepening at 28 critical points along the river. Prosecutors argue these projects are advancing without comprehensive impact assessments or consultation with Indigenous Guató and Kadiwéu peoples and traditional Pantanal communities, violating international labor conventions. The cumulative effect, they warn, could disrupt the wetland's natural flood pulse, the seasonal rhythm of water flow that sustains the Pantanal's extraordinary biodiversity. The lawsuit also challenges claims of insufficient funding, citing a technical report showing that between 2021 and 2025, the National Water Agency left over 149 million reais unspent and failed to allocate more than a billion reais collected specifically for water resource management. This story highlights a tension familiar in many parts of the world: how to balance economic ambitions with environmental stewardship, especially in places recognized as global treasures. The Pantanal holds constitutional protection in Brazil and international designations from UNESCO, yet its governance remains incomplete. The case is a reminder that protecting irreplaceable landscapes often requires not just laws on paper, but the institutions and voices to bring those laws to life.

The unlikely rise of the sea shanty band

Sea shanties, the rhythmic working songs once sung by 19th-century sailors to coordinate grueling shipboard labor, are experiencing an unexpected revival across the United Kingdom. The resurgence began in 2021 when Scottish postman Nathan Evans's rendition of "Wellerman" went viral on TikTok, sparking a social media craze that introduced these maritime melodies to a new generation. What started as an online phenomenon has blossomed into something more enduring: hundreds of community shanty groups have formed in coastal towns and even inland cities, drawing singers who never imagined themselves performing in public. Tony Lewis, an operations manager at a lifeboat station in Newhaven, exemplifies this trend. He joined a local group called the Wreckers despite having no prior singing experience, and now their Wednesday night rehearsals in a garden shed have become the highlight of his week. While the singers tend to be men over 40, the audiences span all ages—children sing along at the front while teenagers and young adults fill the back. The Falmouth International Sea Shanty Festival now attracts over 65,000 visitors, with organizers noting unprecedented youth attendance. Brighton's Homeward Bound even hosts sea shanty workshops for wedding parties at craft beer venues. This revival represents more than nostalgia or novelty. For participants like Lewis, shanty singing maintains a living connection to maritime heritage and coastal identity at a time when few people work directly with the sea. The communal, participatory nature of shanties—designed to unite crews through call-and-response—translates beautifully to modern community building. In an era of algorithmically curated individual listening, these "rum-bunctious" group performances offer something quietly radical: the simple pleasure of raising voices together in shared purpose.

Hawke's Bay community makes big effort to restore native A'Deane's Bush

In rural Hawke's Bay, New Zealand, a dedicated community is quietly working to restore A'Deane's Bush, a 40-hectare remnant of the original podocarp forest that once covered the Ruataniwha Plains. The bush is home to one of the country's largest totara trees, a threatened colony of long-tailed bats, and a rare native mistletoe. What makes this restoration effort particularly special is its collaborative spirit: local landowners John and Jay Benton provide steady funding, conservation leader Kay Griffiths coordinates the work, and the Department of Conservation partners through a management agreement that became a model for similar projects nationwide. The bush nearly disappeared in the 1980s when a farm owner threatened to clear it for grazing, but was persuaded to sell to DOC instead. Since then, volunteers have cleared invasive blackberry and planted thousands of native seedlings, with 500 to 700 plants added each year during community planting days. Students from Sherwood School grow plants in their shade house and participate in regular plantings, some having worked in the bush since they were five years old. The surrounding White family property provides a crucial buffer zone where extensive pest control protects the bat colony, 80 percent of whose roosts are concentrated within A'Deane's relatively small area. This story quietly illustrates how conservation succeeds when commitment runs deep and wide—from an 86-year-old volunteer who has dedicated 26 years to environmental work, to young families earning Duke of Edinburgh hours, to landowners investing in habitat restoration. It's a reminder that protecting biodiversity often depends less on grand gestures than on steady, multigenerational care for the places we call home.

‘Lost’ for 170 years, rare plant recorded in Sri Lanka

In a small forest fragment along Sri Lanka's Sitawaka Ganga River, researchers have rediscovered a plant that hasn't been seen in the country since 1855. Indianthus virgatus, a delicate species with small white flowers that grows in the shaded understory of wet tropical forests, was thought to possibly be extinct in Sri Lanka, though it persists at around 150 locations in India. Using historical records and predictive habitat modeling, a research team pinpointed likely spots in southwestern Sri Lanka's Sabaragamuwa Province, and in January 2025, they found a population of 70 to 100 individuals exactly where their models predicted. What makes this discovery particularly intriguing is that I. virgatus is the sole member of its genus, and its populations are separated by a significant geographical gap between India and Sri Lanka. This disjunct distribution raises fascinating questions: did an ancient geological event split a once-continuous population, or did the plant reach Sri Lanka through long-distance dispersal? The researchers believe the species survived undetected for 170 years in sheltered pockets of moist, shaded forest near streams and slopes—microclimates that remained stable even as surrounding landscapes were dramatically altered. This rediscovery underscores the quiet importance of small forest remnants that might seem insignificant at first glance. Most suitable habitat for I. virgatus in Sri Lanka has been lost to tea and rubber plantations, making protection of these micro-refugia urgent. The finding reminds us that patient, methodical fieldwork guided by scientific modeling can still yield remarkable surprises, and that even fragments of forest may harbor species waiting silently to be found again after more than a century and a half.

Researchers from the Cawthron Institute and Callaghan Innovation are combing pristine coastal areas, sub-Antarctic zones, and even the waters around Whakaari White Island, collecting samples of marine microalgae and bacteria that might hold the key to next-generation sunscreens, anti-aging creams, and other beauty formulations. Any commercial benefits will be shared with participating Māori communities, and all genomic information will remain under New Zealand stewardship. Philip Fearnside, an American researcher who has spent half a century studying the Amazon rainforest, recently received tribute from colleagues and former students at Brazil's National Institute for Amazonian Research. The recognition highlighted decades of meticulous work calculating the true costs of development projects in the world's largest rainforest—from agricultural settlements along the Trans-Amazonian Highway to controversial dam projects and road construction. Fearnside's research has consistently challenged official narratives about the Amazon's economic potential, producing influential findings on deforestation, forest carbon storage, and infrastructure impacts that informed the IPCC's climate work. 'Tears of joy': Woman's lost thumb replaced with second toe

When Francisca Amaral lost her left thumb in a conveyor belt accident at a Queensland produce factory, the 40-year-old East Timorese migrant worker feared for her future. She supports not only herself but her partner, two sons, mother, and siblings back in East Timor—making the injury in January particularly frightening. Eight months later, she has a functioning thumb again, thanks to a remarkable 12-hour surgery that transferred her second toe to her hand. Plastic surgeon Chandan Jadhav performed the Sunshine Coast's first toe-to-thumb transfer in July, a procedure requiring extraordinary precision. The surgeon, who had performed similar operations in India 15 years earlier, took care to prepare Amaral mentally for the three-to-six-month lead-up, acknowledging the psychological weight of such life-changing trauma. For Amaral, who woke in pain but filled with hope and "tears of joy," the surgery promises to restore roughly 80 percent of her thumb function and more than half her overall hand capability. It's a reminder that behind complex procedures are real lives—and sometimes, the most meaningful innovations happen not in headlines, but in the steady, painstaking work of rebuilding what was lost.

"Are we alone in the universe?": the mysteries of space that NASA's ultra-powerful Roman telescope seeks to answer

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched successfully from Florida this Sunday, embarking on a 100-day journey to an observation point roughly 1.6 million kilometers from Earth. Named after NASA's first female executive and chief astronomer from the 1960s, the telescope promises to dramatically expand our view of the cosmos with a field of vision 100 times wider than both the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes. The Roman telescope's primary mission addresses one of humanity's most enduring questions: are we alone in the universe? Scientists expect it to discover tens of thousands—perhaps even 100,000—new exoplanets, worlds orbiting stars beyond our solar system. Operating at a distance four times farther than the Moon, the telescope will use infrared cameras to capture what astronomers call "thermal light," positioning itself far enough to avoid interference from Earth and lunar radiation. Beyond planet hunting, Roman will investigate some of the universe's deepest mysteries, including dark energy, dark matter, and black holes, while mapping billions of galaxies across space. What makes this story quietly remarkable is how it builds on decades of astronomical achievement while opening entirely new windows into the cosmos. The telescope honors a pioneer who helped bring the Hubble to fruition, and now her namesake instrument will search for answers she herself found most intriguing. With an initial five-year mission and hopes for ten years of operation, Roman represents humanity's patient, persistent effort to understand our place in an incomprehensibly vast universe—one exoplanet at a time.

How GPS, Created for War, Shaped the Modern World

A curious incident in 2017 offers a window into one of the modern world's most ubiquitous yet least noticed technologies. Several oil tankers approaching a Russian port discovered their GPS systems showed them hovering in mid-air over a nearby airport, even as their eyes confirmed they were sailing on water. This bizarre glitch sparked journalist Katherine Dunn's deep dive into GPS, the satellite-based system that quietly shapes nearly every aspect of contemporary life. What began as a military tool for precision bombing during the Vietnam War has evolved into the invisible infrastructure of global civilization. GPS does far more than help us navigate to unfamiliar addresses. It synchronizes cell phone towers, banking systems, and electrical grids, relying on atomic clocks accurate to billionths of a second. The system works by having devices receive signals from four satellites simultaneously, solving equations for longitude, latitude, altitude, and time. This time-keeping function is crucial: every smartphone essentially carries a pocket atomic clock, enabling the split-second coordination that modern digital life demands. From agricultural precision to traffic light timing, from online shopping delivery to international shipping logistics, GPS threads through systems we take for granted. This story matters because it reveals how a technology born from conflict has become so deeply woven into daily existence that we barely notice it—until it goes wrong. That little blue dot on our screens represents more than our location; it's become how we identify ourselves in digital space, a new form of "I" that required no instruction manual to understand. Understanding GPS means understanding the hidden scaffolding of the modern world.

The geriatric giant growing by the hour

New Zealand faces a quietly momentous challenge: the number of people living with dementia is projected to more than double over the next 25 years, rising from nearly 83,000 in 2025 to 167,400 by 2050. Every hour, three people develop the condition—a number expected to climb to four per hour. The economic burden will mirror this growth, doubling from $3.2 billion to $6.4 billion. Māori, Pacific, and Asian communities are seeing particularly rapid increases in dementia rates. Yet amid these sobering projections, geriatrician Dr. Cheryl Johnson sees reason for hope. She points to everyday scenes—like elderly volunteers helping schoolchildren cross a busy road in Auckland—as small but powerful examples of what matters most: connection, purpose, and community engagement. These elements, along with a Mediterranean diet, regular exercise, moderate alcohol use, and activities that stimulate the brain, can significantly reduce dementia risk. According to recent research, 40 percent of dementia cases stem from modifiable factors that can be identified and addressed. One in three diagnoses are preceded by mild cognitive impairment, a critical window for intervention, and nearly a quarter of those referred for memory concerns turn out to have reversible conditions, not dementia. This story matters because it reframes a growing health crisis not as inevitable decline, but as an opportunity for early action and lifestyle change. With disease-modifying therapies on the horizon and increasing understanding of prevention, the message is both urgent and encouraging: the choices people make today—getting a hearing test, learning a language, staying socially active—can profoundly shape their cognitive futures.

Once threatened, humpback whales abound on the Brazilian coast

Off the coast of Brazil, in the South Atlantic's largest humpback whale breeding sanctuary, a scene once unimaginable unfolds: males compete energetically for females, their tails slapping the water as they jostle for position. Just decades ago, humpback whales were nearly extinct in these waters. Today, roughly 35,000 individuals—nearly half the global population—thrive here, a remarkable turnaround achieved through hunting bans, habitat protection, and dedicated research. The Humpback Whale Institute, founded in 1996 and based in Caravelas in southern Bahia, leads much of this conservation work. Between June and November, researchers journey to the Abrolhos archipelago, about 70 kilometers offshore, where warm waters provide ideal conditions for females to give birth and nurse their calves. Using biopsy darts, the team collects skin and blubber samples that reveal family connections and migration patterns. One discovery linked a whale born in Abrolhos to a relative spotted near South Georgia Island, 4,000 kilometers south, helping map the species' journey from summer feeding grounds in the far southern Atlantic to Brazilian breeding waters. Artificial intelligence has revolutionized their work: the Happy Whale platform now identifies individual whales in seconds by their unique tail patterns, a task that once required countless hours of manual comparison. The system has cataloged 8,300 Brazilian humpbacks and even documented a record-breaking 15,000-kilometer journey to Australia's east coast. This story offers a rare and heartening example of successful conservation, showing how protection efforts and scientific curiosity can bring a species back from the brink—transforming what were once legends into a living, breathing abundance.

For decades, researchers have observed a curious pattern: children who grow up on farms develop asthma, hay fever, and eczema far less often than their urban peers. This process dampens inflammatory responses and reduces allergy risk. The nine identified bacteria explain roughly two-thirds of the protective effect against asthma and about half the effect for hay fever and eczema. Timing matters, too: the most critical window appears to be the first years of life, possibly even beginning before birth when pregnant mothers spend time in barn environments. This research offers more than an explanation for why farm children breathe easier—it points toward a more precise understanding of how our immune systems learn to distinguish real threats from harmless triggers. The famous "weep" inscription from 1904 represents just one chapter in a much longer chronicle of drought. These stones have captured renewed attention during recent European droughts in 2020 and 2022, with media describing them as ominous harbingers. Yet they're perhaps better understood as a bridge between past and present—a reminder that communities have long grappled with water scarcity, and found ways to document their struggles for future generations. In an era of climate uncertainty, these submerged chronicles offer both historical perspective and quiet testament to human resilience.

"Amicable numbers", the strange mathematical pairs that have captivated lovers, mystics and scientists for 2,500 years

For over 2,500 years, a curious mathematical phenomenon has captivated philosophers, mystics, and mathematicians alike: amicable numbers. These are pairs of numbers where each holds the exact identity of the other through their divisors. Take 220 and 284—the divisors of 220 sum to 284, and the divisors of 284 sum to 220. This elegant reciprocity, first documented by the Syrian philosopher Iamblichus and attributed to Pythagoras, seemed to embody the ancient saying "a friend is another self." But these numbers didn't remain confined to mathematical treatises. Across cultures and centuries, people infused them with mystical meaning. Jewish Kabbalists noted that when Jacob sent his estranged brother Esau a peace offering, it included precisely 220 goats and 220 sheep—interpreted as a numerical charm to invoke forgiveness and fraternal love. Islamic scholars and medieval grimoires prescribed talismans inscribed with 220 and 284 to forge friendship or romantic bonds between two people. The belief persisted that these numbers could not merely symbolize affection but actually conjure it. What makes this story quietly remarkable is how a purely mathematical curiosity became a canvas for human longing across vastly different traditions. The same pairs of numbers that intrigued rational mathematicians also carried the hopes of lovers and the prayers of brothers seeking reconciliation. It's a reminder that even in the abstract world of number theory, people have always searched for patterns that reflect our deepest relationships—and sometimes dared to believe that understanding those patterns might help us shape them.
